author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Organize storage and scan a PS2 library
summary: Build a predictable Android folder layout, grant durable access, scan multiple locations without duplicates, and recover from moved folders or removable-storage failures.
heroAlt: EmuCoreX library showing a grid of detected PlayStation 2 games

blocks.text: Design the folders before the scan

Treat game images, emulator data and temporary downloads as different classes of storage. Put verified PS2 images under a stable library root, keep BIOS files in a private firmware folder, and let the emulator-data root hold memory cards, states, patches, textures and logs. This separation prevents a library refresh from crawling backups or showing duplicate working copies.
Do not scan a folder that also contains unpacking targets, cloud-sync conflict copies or backup mirrors. A clean library root should contain only the images you intend to launch.

Before adding folders, remove partial downloads and confirm that every image has a unique, meaningful filename. If internal storage and an SD card are both used, give each a distinct top-level folder. Android grants access to the chosen document-tree URI; that permission follows the selected tree, not a path typed into another app.

items: Verified personal game images in supported formats.
One stable library folder per storage device.
Enough free space for covers, metadata and save data outside the game folder.
A mounted SD card, if used, that Android reports without errors.
A backup of the existing emulator-data folder before restructuring.

blocks.text: Add, scan and label each location

items: 1. Create a PS2 library root and move only verified launchable images into it; use subfolders for region or collection only when they improve navigation.
2. Open EmuCoreX setup or Settings, choose Add game folders, and grant access to the library root through Android's picker.
3. Add a second root only when it points to different content, such as an SD-card collection. Do not add both a parent and its child.
4. Run refresh and wait until scanning and metadata work settle. Check several entries for the expected serial, cover and file location.
5. Favorite or tag a small test set, restart the app, and confirm that the same entries remain linked to the same files.

blocks.text: Compare the number of physical images with the number of library entries after accounting for multidisc sets. Open a title from each storage root. A correct scan should not require rescanning after every launch, should preserve favorites and should show no second entry merely because a parent folder overlaps a child folder.

items: No folder is nested inside another selected folder.
One entry resolves to one working image location.
Internal and removable-storage games both cold-start.
Favorites and recent-game state survive an app restart.
Removing an SD card produces a clear unavailable-folder state rather than deleting unrelated entries.

blocks.text: If a reorganization creates duplicates, remove the overlapping folder permission first and refresh before deleting files. When a folder was moved, reselect its new location and verify saves before removing the old tree. If an SD card becomes unreliable, copy verified images to healthy storage and rebuild that root; never move the emulator-data folder and the game library simultaneously.

items: Revoke the newest overlapping root and refresh.
Restore the previous folder layout from backup when URI permissions cannot be repaired.
Reinsert and remount removable storage before changing library records.
Keep cover-cache problems separate from file-detection problems; refresh metadata only after paths work.
Every game appears twice: parent and child trees were both selected.
Games vanish after reboot: transient provider or removable-storage access was used.
Scan never settles: backup archives or a download folder are inside the library root.
Title opens the wrong region: ambiguous filenames hide two distinct images.

blocks.text: A disciplined folder tree makes later troubleshooting much cheaper. When an entry fails, you can identify its device, file and permission without touching BIOS, graphics or saves. Document the two or three roots you deliberately selected and change one root at a time when the collection grows.
